client: Hey Luna, I’ve been really stressed out lately. I’m preparing for my final exams next month, and I’m especially worried about chemistry because I really struggled with it last semester. I feel like I’m not making any progress, and it’s starting to overwhelm me. I’m not even sure if talking about it will help, but here I am.
therapist: Hi there, I’m really glad you reached out and shared this with me. It sounds like you’re under a lot of pressure, especially with chemistry, and it’s completely understandable to feel overwhelmed. How are you coping with these feelings, and are there any small steps you think might help ease the stress, even a little bit?

client: Thanks for listening, Luna. To be honest, I’ve been trying to study more, but it feels like no matter how much I do, it’s never enough. I’ve also been staying up late, which isn’t helping my anxiety. I’m not sure if there’s a way to make it easier—I feel like I’m just stuck in this cycle of stress and worry. It’s hard to see a way out.
therapist: I can hear how exhausting and frustrating this feels for you, and it’s really brave of you to share this. It’s understandable that you feel stuck, but it’s important to remember that small changes can sometimes make a big difference. Have you noticed any moments, however brief, where you felt a little less overwhelmed or more in control? What was different during those times?

client: That’s a good question, Luna. I think there were a couple of times when I felt a bit better. One was when I studied with a friend, and another was when I took a break to go for a walk. I guess having some company or just a change of scenery helped, but it’s hard to make those things happen consistently when I’m so focused on studying. I don’t want to fall behind, but I also know I can’t keep pushing myself this hard.
therapist: It’s really insightful of you to recognize those moments that helped, even if they were brief. It sounds like having support and taking breaks can make a positive difference. Maybe we can explore ways to incorporate these more regularly into your routine, even in small doses. What do you think about setting aside a short, regular time each day for a walk or a quick chat with a friend, just to give yourself a mental break? How might that feel for you?

client: I appreciate the suggestion, Luna, but I’m worried that taking breaks might make me feel guilty or like I’m not doing enough. I know it’s important to rest, but it’s hard to find the balance when I feel like I’m already behind. I’m afraid that if I take too many breaks, I won’t be able to catch up, and that just adds to my anxiety.
therapist: I completely understand where you’re coming from, and it’s totally normal to feel that way. It’s a tough balance to strike, but it’s important to remember that taking breaks can actually improve your focus and productivity in the long run. Maybe we can start with very short breaks, like a 5-10 minute walk or a quick chat, and see how that feels. What do you think about trying this for a few days and then reflecting on how it impacts your study sessions and overall stress levels?

client: I see your point, Luna, and I’m willing to give it a try. I guess I can start with those short breaks and see how it goes. It’s just hard to shake off that guilt, but I’ll do my best to remind myself that it might actually help me in the long run. Let’s see how it feels after a few days.
therapist: That’s a great attitude to have, and I’m really proud of you for being open to trying something new. It’s completely normal to feel some guilt at first, but giving yourself permission to take those breaks can be a powerful step toward managing your stress. After a few days, we can check in and see how it’s going. How does that sound? And in the meantime, what’s one small thing you can tell yourself to help reinforce the idea that taking breaks is beneficial?

client: Thanks, Luna. It does feel good to have some support. I think I can tell myself something like, "Taking a break will help me focus better and reduce my stress." It’s a simple reminder, but I hope it helps me feel less guilty. I’ll give it a try and let you know how it goes.
therapist: That’s a wonderful reminder, and I’m sure it will make a difference. It’s great to have a simple, positive phrase to come back to when those guilty feelings arise. I’m here for you, and I’m looking forward to hearing how it goes. How about we also touch base on any other thoughts or feelings that come up as you try this new approach?

client: I really appreciate your support, Luna. I’ll keep an eye on my thoughts and feelings as I try this new approach. It’s a bit scary to step out of my comfort zone, but I’m willing to give it a shot and see if it makes a difference. I’ll let you know how it goes.
therapist: I’m so glad to hear that you’re willing to give it a try, and I’m here to support you every step of the way. It’s completely normal to feel a bit scared when trying something new, but you’re already showing immense courage and resilience. I’m excited to hear about your progress and any insights you gain along the way. How about we also think about what might help you feel more comfortable and confident as you take these steps?

client: Thanks, Luna. Thinking about what might help me feel more comfortable and confident is a good idea. Maybe if I can find a specific time each day for these breaks, it will feel more structured and less like I’m just avoiding my work. I’ll try to set a timer or something to remind me to take these breaks. It’s a small step, but I think it could help.
therapist: That’s a fantastic plan, and setting a specific time with a timer is a great way to make it feel more structured and manageable. It can help take the pressure off and make the breaks feel like a natural part of your routine. How does it feel to have this plan in place, and is there anything else you think might support you as you start implementing these breaks?

client: It feels a bit more manageable now, knowing I have a plan. I’m still a little nervous about sticking to it, but having a specific time and a timer should help. I think it would also be helpful to have a small reward after I complete my study sessions, maybe something simple like a favorite snack or a short episode of a show I enjoy. It might make it easier to stick to the breaks.
therapist: That’s a wonderful idea, and adding a small reward can definitely make sticking to your plan more enjoyable and motivating. It’s great that you’re thinking about ways to make this process more positive for yourself. How do you think these rewards might impact your overall study routine and stress levels? And is there anything else you’d like to consider as you move forward with this plan?

client: I think the rewards could really help me stay motivated and make the breaks feel more rewarding. It might reduce some of my anxiety because I’ll have something to look forward to. The only thing I’m still a bit worried about is finding the right balance—making sure the rewards don’t become a distraction. But I’ll give it a try and see how it goes.
therapist: It’s great to hear that you’re feeling more motivated, and using rewards is a smart strategy to help reduce anxiety and make the breaks more enjoyable. Finding the right balance is definitely important, and it’s okay to adjust things as you go. Maybe you can start with small, quick rewards that you know won’t take too much time, and see how that feels. How do you think you’ll know if a reward is working well for you, and is there a specific sign you’ll look for to tell if it’s helping with your study routine?
